en: Having received the prince's* blessing,
Asking gracious Allah to grant a road,
With a spare courser made ready,
Your valiant uncle Bakai
Took the champion hero with him,
And Külchoro and Kanchoro,
The two matched lions.
"I shall gird my waist firmly;
For Kongurbai in Beijing
I shall pursue the blood-price
Of my valiant father Khan Manas,
And lions Chubak and Almambet.
How could a nobleman's* son
Go on without taking revenge?!
My valiant uncle, where is the road?!
The Kakanchin are those I shall fight,
Bakburchun those I shall confront;
There is no remedy against fate.
At the house built in Kerüü,
Lion uncle, we have made ready
Against the mighty khan of the monks!
Let us set our faces and level our spears
Toward the mighty city of Beijing!
If death reaches us, let us die;
Against the infidel son of the kalday,
Let us set out on holy war
Against hero Khan Kongurbai!"
Committing himself to fate, he spoke;
Old Bakai, mountainlike, said:
"The road to Beijing divides five ways;
We shall choose one and see what we meet!
Wherever we arrive, we shall press on;
If we grapple with the infidel,
Hero Khan Kongurbai,
We shall spill his blood!
Entering Beijing is a toilsome task;
There are countless black cattle gathered as tribute,
And tens of thousands of treasury livestock;
At the very least, we shall raid
The infidel's horses and escape!
It has a kalday and a khan,
And every kind of foe to fight.
There lies the land of Chin-Machin;
If Bakai speaks the truth,
His true account is inexhaustible!
The road to Beijing divides five ways;
Fix this firmly in mind, my son!
When Bakai cries out his warning,
He knows horrors no mortal has heard!
The road to Beijing has five branches;
There is no mortal who has traveled all five—
So formidable are they, splendid hero!
On one road to Beijing,
Whoever goes does not return—a calamitous road.
There is one road to Beijing
Where whoever meets it never comes back—a dark road!
There is one road to Beijing
Where the mortal who sets out upon it
Wanders and dies—a dark road!
There is one road to Beijing
With a pass that has been sealed shut;
On one road to Beijing
There are guards and a khan;
On one road to Beijing
Are every kind of devourer!
It has its obstacles and its lore;
When we go upon that road,
Do not grieve me, son—heed my words!
Its people have giants;
What does accursed Beijing
Not possess within it!
Its people are of many kinds;
Foxes keep watch upon its passes.
There is a champion appointed from among the monks,
And surpassing swift beings
Who let no mounted soul escape!
There is a lake where ducks lie,
It has a pass where white argali lie.
That fire-doomed swine
Has a lion who passes judgment!
It has a land where fanged beasts lie;
Accursed Beijing
There is a forty-day desert!
The other side of that desert
Chok-Tabylgy makes his summer camp,
Tied up his big black horse,
The youngest of sixty kaldays,
A pure-blooded younger kinsman of Alöökö,
And chief of the monks.
In Kerüü there is a surety-house;
With cotton sash and broad boots,
They have a mighty khan of the Kechil,
That is the enemy you will contend with!
There is a tiger born and bred,
And that fire-doomed swine's
There is also a miracle.
When you set your face toward Beijing,
There are wonders for mortals to see;
While my lord Manas was alive,
Did your valiant uncle Bakai
Not gird himself for such deeds?!"
Roused upon Kökcholok,
Your uncle Bakai the gray wolf
He took a blue spear,
Praying to the Creator
Put on a blue lynx-fur cap,
And bore the blue-mottled shield and banner.
In Bakai's hand
Was a golden-cheeked battle-axe;
At Bakai's left side
Was a pouch made of gold.
His foe was the Kakanchin;
Bakai separated from Talas,
Your uncle Bakai then
Loomed like Ala-Too.
Across the broad back
Of your lion Bakai
The firearm Kök Chybuk gleamed;
In the scabbard of your dear uncle Bakai,
The sword clanged in its scabbard.
The sight arrested the heart;
Your lion uncle Bakai's
Form and majesty,
His bearing on horseback,
Appeared equal to a thousand troops.
Then Bakai's white beard
Spread apart,
Divided to the right and left,
And your uncle Bakai
Appeared in the form of a saint;
Renowned as a true saint—
Was that not Bakai,
Who, while lion Manas was alive,
Learned the ways of fighting Kakan—
Was that not Bakai?
Your uncle Bakai led the way;
The sight arrested the heart,
And though your uncle was old,
His gray-wolf nature showed.
Old Bakai was one,
Kulchoro and Kanchoro
The younger kinsmen of lion Semetey.
Driving fourteen horses
He had the golden tent folded,
Loaded it upon each bay horse,
And had all the ammunition
Loaded upon fourteen horses;
He had the paired saddle-straps drawn tight—
When setting out against the enemy,
Dear Bakai and Külchoro,
Retainers of the bloodthirsty hero.
Heading to Beijing
Beren Semetey, the gray wolf,
Set out from Talas.
The Kyrgyz and Argyn people wept,
And both mothers of the gray wolf wept.
The Argyn and Kyrgyz then,
Raising their palms and wailing,
Prayed that the noble hero be kept safe.
They prayed, sobbing.
The splendid lion, son of Manas,
Wore a coat no bullet could pierce,
And rode a horse no bullet could catch;
He turned Buurul obliquely
And knotted his horsehair tail tight.
Buurul was the steed beneath him,
And he had the strength to strike Beijing,
Which no raider could touch, alone!
Akolpok shines on his back,
When set to shooting, the heirloom
Akelte shines on the back,
The sight arrested the heart;
Half bronze and half gold,
A gray pouch is visible on the waist,
The white sighthound barked behind him,
And Akshumkar cried out upon his hand.
A golden-cheeked battle-axe,
Forged of steel and sharpened keen,
Its handle wound about with yellow gold,
Kakanchyn's Beijing
To strike in the battle for Beijing,
Had been repaired by smith Bölökbai.
If you ask about the sword,
The six-edged blade fallen from heaven,
Zulfiqar, left as a gift
By valiant Manas, the gray wolf.
Zulfiqar rang in its sheath;
Semetei who took the sword
Stood ringing like Opol-Too.
Standing erect and untroubled,
He reckoned the Black Chinese he would fight,
And the thought that he might finally die,
As less than the hem of his robe!
Heroism and leonine courage
The Almighty Allah
Had granted the lion's son
Without measure.
Heading towards Beijing
Riding hard and covering much ground,
Traveling not a little but far,
Crossing rounded, arching passes,
Traversing many kinds of country,
Past straight-flowing springs and clear water,
He journeyed without stopping or resting,
Riding hard and pressing far,
Wearying horses and scouting the land,
Running hounds and flying birds—
Your young son of the Bloodthirsty One
Was journeying toward Kakan.
He crossed rugged passes,
Passed over many turning uplands,
And skirted the mountain foothills;
Your gray wolf journeyed on,
Roaming through Ala-Too,
Crossing Kötörmö,
And traversing broad Suusamyr.
By the mountain of Kyz-Art,
For his coming battle with Great Beijing,
Your gray wolf had
All the fine thoroughbreds
Shod with steel.
Along deserted Elkin-Too,
He skirted Elkin-Too;
He bent down and looked
A blue lake appeared,
And the many ducks resting on the lake
Scattered when a falcon struck.
Ah, wondrous Issyk-Köl—
Is it not the rump of the earth?
Would anyone dwelling here ever leave?!
It has its Küngöi and its Teskei,
With mountains rising into view;
When one looks toward their foothills,
The human heart is overcome.
On its slopes pines grow thick in heaps,
And crystal-clear springs pour from the hollows.
Its bounty is complete;
God willing
It's a memorable place!
Are its summer pastures not nearby?
Would the Kyrgyz not settle there for summer!
Are its winter quarters not nearby?
Would the Kyrgyz not winter there!
Roe deer cry from the slopes,
And owls call from the rugged ground.
It's a blessed place,
Its hillsides bear fescue and wormwood.
The great Kyrgyz people would choose it
It was a place to stay.
With kumis by day and girls by night,
It's a place to be.
Ah, wondrous Issyk-Köl—
Is it not the rump of the earth?
Would any mortal dwelling there ever leave?!
Looking toward the Küngöi side—
Haze lies over Chaar-Tal;
